query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-heating the substrate during laser powder bed fusion (SLM) of high-entropy alloys will reduce thermal gradients and residual stresses, thereby improving dimensional precision, enhancing mechanical integrity, and reducing defects such as pores and hot cracking.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built high-entropy alloy components (e.g., CoCrFeNiCu or CoCrFeNiMn alloys) produced by conventional SLM processes at room-temperature substrate conditions, which exhibit significant residual stresses, cracking, and porosity.
generation.intervention: Implement a controlled substrate pre-heating step during the SLM process (e.g., raising the substrate temperature to an optimized elevated level) while keeping other process parameters constant.
generation.conditions: SLM processing conducted in an inert atmosphere with fixed laser power, scan speed, and powder characteristics. The intervention should be tested within a pre-heating temperature range (for example, approximately 200–500 °C) on high-entropy alloy components with complex geometries.
generation.structural_mediator: By reducing the thermal gradient during rapid melting and solidification, pre-heating leads to lower residual stresses and refined microstructure; this in turn minimizes the formation of process-induced defects such as porosity and hot cracks and improves dimensional stability.
generation.mechanism: Pre-heating the substrate mitigates the steep thermal gradients intrinsic to SLM. This slower cooling reduces residual stress accumulation and prevents abrupt solidification anomalies (e.g., hot cracking or pore formation), thus yielding parts with more uniform microstructure and better dimensional fidelity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline (room-temperature substrate), the pre-heated builds are expected to display fewer defects, enhanced dimensional precision, and improved mechanical properties (e.g., higher yield strength and better ductility); however, the exact magnitude of these improvements remains to be quantified.
generation.baseline: Components produced by SLM under standard processing conditions with a room-temperature substrate, which typically exhibit significant residual stresses, non-uniform microstructures, and increased defect densities.
generation.boundary: The efficacy of pre-heating may depend on the specific high-entropy alloy composition and may require tuning of temperature levels; very high-melting-point alloys or those with highly sensitive phase equilibria might show different responses.
generation.uncertainty: While the overall trend of defect reduction and mechanical improvement is supported, the precise quantitative enhancements (e.g., percentage reduction in defects or exact improvement in mechanical properties) are uncertain without dedicated experimental studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of high-entropy alloy components using SLM under identical processing conditions except for substrate temperature. One set is built using a pre-heated substrate (e.g., maintained at an optimized temperature between 200–500 °C) and the other using the conventional room-temperature substrate. Ensure all other parameters (laser power, scan speed, powder characteristics, etc.) are constant. Post-fabrication, perform a comparative analysis of dimensional accuracy, residual stress distribution, defect density (pores, cracks), and mechanical properties.
measurements: 3D metrological analysis (e.g., laser scanning or profilometry) to assess dimensional precision
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) for microstructural characterization and detection of defects
Mechanical tests (e.g., tensile strength, yield strength, ductility, hardness)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-heated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in defect density, improved dimensional accuracy, and enhanced mechanical properties compared to the control (room-temperature substrate) beyond the experimental uncertainty, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The precise nature of the hot-cracking mechanism, whether it be solidification or liquation cracking, remains ambiguous. Compared to previous studies, our findings both align with and extend the current understanding of hot-cracking in HEAs. Notably, Sun et al. [] reported that in additively manufactured CoCrFeNi alloys, intergranular hot cracks are primarily associated with large columnar grains and high residual stresses, with minimal elemental segregation at grain boundaries. In contrast, our study on CoCrFeNiCu reveals pronounced segregation of Cu and Mn at HAGBs, suggesting the persistence of a liquid film at the end of solidification and a greater role for elemental segregation in promoting hot-cracking in Cu-containing HEAs. This is consistent with recent work showing that strong Cu segregation during solidification promotes hot-cracking in AlCoCrCuyFeNi alloys, as Cu-rich liquid films facilitate solidification and liquation cracking [].

This study uniquely demonstrates the processability, hot-cracking susceptibility, and in situ mechanical response of CoCrFeNiCu-HEA fabricated by L-PBF, providing new insights into defect evolution and mechanical performance under these specific processing conditions. Future work will focus on targeted alloying (e.g., Al addition), pre-heating strategies, and optimized scanning to further reduce hot-cracking susceptibility and enhance mechanical performance. This study provides insights into the processability, defect evolution, and mechanical response of L-PBF CoCrFeNiCu-HEA, guiding the development of crack-resistant, additively manufactured HEAs.
